dedupe_keys.name: extreme relativistic electron fluxes in gps orbit from ns41 bdd iir data 1 in 10 and 1 in 100 year levels

description: This dataset gives an extreme value analysis of the daily average relativistic electron flux in GPS-type orbit, as a function of energy and L shell, from the Burst Detector Dosimeter IIR on the US NS41 GPS satellite between 10 December 2000 and 25 July 2020. It provides the 1 in 10 year and 1 in 100 year flux levels for energies from 0.6 to 8.0 MeV; for example the 1 in 10 year flux at L 4.5 falls from 8.2 million to 33 units as energy rises, and near geostationary orbit (L 6.5) the 1 in 100 year event is 1.1 to 13 times the 1 in 10 year event. The analysis suggests an upper bound for 0.6 to 2 MeV electrons near L 4.5 but largely unbounded fluxes further out. It was prepared by Nigel Meredith of the British Antarctic Survey with Thomas and Michael Cayton, funded by NERC grants including Sat-Risk, and published as downloadable text files by the UK Polar Data Centre in April 2023 under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Caveats: it is a statistical product from one satellite and energy channel set, extrapolation to 1 in 100 years carries wide uncertainty, and fluxes are orbit averages. It supports reasonable-worst-case radiation specifications for internal charging and dose studies of navigation and telecommunication satellites; a related record is the satellite cable charging worst-case dataset.
